title: psql essentials: \d, \dt, \x, \timing, \e
summary: psql's backslash commands are answered by psql itself, mostly by sending catalog queries it writes for you. Learn the dozen you'll use daily, and the SQL behind \d, which you can reuse anywhere psql isn't.

examples.title: \d without a pattern, as the SQL psql sends

annotations.note: The identity columns bring sequences with them, and \d lists them next to the tables: GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is backed by a sequence the table owns.
COMMENT ON stores documentation in the catalog. \dt+ and \d+ show it in their Description column, so a colleague browsing in psql sees it without opening your repository.
The core of what psql runs for \d, trimmed. Start psql with -E (or \set ECHO_HIDDEN on) and it prints the full query before every meta-command: the quickest way to learn the catalogs.

pg_table_is_visible is true when the table's schema is on the search path and no earlier schema has the same name. It is why \dt lists nothing for tables in schemas outside your path; \dt *.* shows every schema.

examples.title: \d orders: columns, constraints, and the portable way

annotations.note: format_type prints the names psql shows, with modifiers: character varying(80), timestamp with time zone. pg_get_expr turns a stored default back into SQL text. Identity columns have no default expression; their attidentity flag says how values arrive.
Positive attnum skips system columns (ctid, xmin, ...). A dropped column only becomes invisible; its slot stays in pg_attribute, flagged attisdropped, until the table is rewritten.

pg_get_constraintdef reconstructs the definition rather than returning what you typed, hence (total >= (0)::numeric). Since PG 18 NOT NULL is stored here too, as contype 'n' constraints with their own names.

information_schema is the SQL standard's catalog: the same query works on other databases. The price: data_type drops the (80) and (10,2) into separate columns, and every Postgres-specific type collapses to ARRAY or USER-DEFINED.

examples.title: Stored names: folding, quotes, and a Turkish letter

annotations.note: Unquoted names fold to lower case; quoted ones are stored exactly. The fold covers ASCII letters only: in this UTF-8 database Şubeler keeps its capital Ş, so şubeler (with ş) is a different name.

Identifiers are limited to 63 bytes, not characters, and each Turkish letter outside ASCII takes two bytes in UTF-8. This 55-character name is one byte too long, so the server cuts it and says so only in a NOTICE.
length counts characters, octet_length bytes: 7 and 8 for Şubeler. The long name came back at 63 bytes, without its final m.
to_regclass parses its argument as SQL would, folding PAYMENTS to payments and keeping "Invoices" as written, and returns NULL instead of raising an error when nothing matches.
Unquoted, Invoices means invoices, which doesn't exist. psql patterns follow the same rule: \dt Invoices finds nothing; \dt "Invoices" finds the table.

use_cases: Inspecting a server you reached over SSH, where there is no GUI: \dn, \dt app.*, \d app.orders
Running migration and seed scripts: psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f migrate.sql
Learning the catalogs: psql -E prints the SQL behind every meta-command, ready to reuse in Go or TS tooling
strengths: Ships with every PostgreSQL install and needs nothing but a terminal, unlike GUI clients
Meta-commands are thin wrappers over catalog queries you can see (-E) and copy, not a black box
\x auto switches to one-field-per-line only when a row is wider than the screen; \gx does it for a single query
weaknesses: Meta-commands exist only in psql: pgx, node-postgres and every GUI need the catalog queries instead
Its output is formatted for humans, so scripts should query the catalogs or information_schema rather than parse \d
On Windows, the console code page can garble Turkish characters until it matches what psql expects

pitfalls.title: \dt shows nothing, yet the app works
pitfalls.detail: Without a pattern, \d commands list only objects visible on your search_path. The app's tables are probably in another schema: \dn lists schemas, \dt app.* or \dt *.* finds them.

pitfalls.title: NULL and the empty string look identical
pitfalls.detail: By default psql prints nothing for NULL. Set a visible marker once in your psqlrc.

pitfalls.title: A missing semicolon
pitfalls.detail: SQL is sent only at ';' (or \g). Until then psql keeps buffering, and the prompt changes from playground=> to playground-> to say so. Backslash commands, by contrast, end at the newline.

pitfalls.title: Turkish characters garbled in the Windows console
pitfalls.detail: psql warns at startup when it detects a problematic console code page. The docs' fix: switch the console to your Windows code page (cmd.exe /c chcp 1254 on Turkish Windows, 1252 on Western European ones) and set the console font to Lucida Console.

quiz.q: \dt lists no tables, but the application reads and writes them fine. What's the most likely reason?
options: psql lacks privileges to see them
They live in a schema that isn't on your search_path; try \dt *.*
\dt only shows tables created in the current session
quiz.why: Without a pattern, \d commands show only objects visible on the search path. *.* matches every schema.

quiz.q: What does starting psql with -E do?
options: Runs every statement in its own transaction
Prints the catalog queries that backslash commands send
quiz.why: -E is the same as \set ECHO_HIDDEN on: psql shows each hidden query before running it. Expanded output is -x.

quiz.q: After CREATE TABLE "Invoices" (id int), which psql command lists it?
quiz.why: Patterns fold to lower case like unquoted SQL names; double quotes stop the folding.

quiz.q: Why can't your Go code send \d orders through pgx?
options: Meta-commands are interpreted by psql and never reach the server; send the catalog query instead
quiz.why: The server only understands SQL. psql turns \d into catalog queries before anything is sent.

body:
## Concept

psql reads two kinds of input. SQL is buffered until a `;` and then sent to the server.
Backslash commands (meta-commands) end at the newline and are handled by psql itself;
many of them are just catalog queries psql writes for you. That is why StackLab's runner
can't execute `\d`: it only speaks SQL to the server, as your Go code does. The examples
run the SQL those commands stand for instead.

The working set:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `\l`, `\c db` | list databases; reconnect to another one (a new connection) |
| `\dn`, `\dt`, `\dv`, `\di`, `\df`, `\du` | list schemas, tables, views, indexes, functions, roles |
| `\d name`, `\d+ name` | describe one object; `+` adds sizes, comments and more |
| `\x`, `\x auto`, `\gx` | expanded output (one field per line): toggle, only when too wide, or for one query |
| `\timing` | toggle printing how long each statement took |
| `\e`, `\ef fn` | edit the query buffer (or a function) in your editor |
| `\i file.sql` | run a file as if you'd typed it |
| `\?`, `\h CREATE TABLE` | help for meta-commands; SQL syntax help |

Patterns work on every `\d` command: `\dt app.*` lists tables in schema `app`, `\dt *.*`
lists tables in all schemas, and an `S` (`\dtS`) includes system objects.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python's or Node's REPL**: psql is that for SQL, with `\d` in place of `dir()` and
  `help()`, and `\i file.sql` to load a script into the session.
- **The `go` command**: psql ships with the server the way `go` ships with Go. GUI
  clients are optional; psql is always there, including on a server you reach over SSH.
- **Reflection** (Java's `Class.getDeclaredFields`, Go's `reflect`): the system catalogs
  are the database describing itself in tables, and `\d` is a pretty-printer over them.
  `information_schema` is the portable, standardized layer on top, with less detail.
- **Windows**: psql is a console program, and the console has its own code page. If psql
  warns about it at startup, fix that first (see the pitfall), or Turkish letters may
  come out garbled.

## How it works

`\timing` prints how long each statement took as psql saw it, so the number includes the
network and transferring the result, but not printing it. The docs say only "how long
each SQL statement takes"; psql's source (src/bin/psql/common.c, function
ExecQueryAndProcessResults) starts the clock before sending the query and stops it once
the result has arrived, before printing. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, covered in the indexes
module, works the other way round: its Execution Time is measured inside the server and,
per the docs, includes neither planning (reported separately) nor sending rows to the
client. When `\timing` is much larger, the gap is planning plus getting the rows to you.
On PostgreSQL 18.7 here, 300,000 generated rows sent to `\o NUL` took 135 to 184 ms by
`\timing`, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of the same query reported 61 to 81 ms.

`\e` opens the current query buffer (or, if it's empty, the last query) in an editor:
`PSQL_EDITOR`, `EDITOR` or `VISUAL`, whichever is set first, else `vi` on Unix and
`notepad.exe` on Windows. When you save and quit, any complete statement in the buffer,
one ending in `;`, runs at once. Your personal settings go in `~/.psqlrc`, or
`%APPDATA%\postgresql\psqlrc.conf` on Windows; `\x auto`, `\timing on` and a
`\pset null` marker are common first lines.

Patterns follow SQL's identifier rules: unquoted letters fold to lower case, double
quotes keep them. In SQL itself, in a UTF-8 database, the server's fold only touches
ASCII letters, as the `Şubeler` example shows. The docs say only that unquoted names "are
always folded to lower case"; the server's source (src/backend/parser/scansup.c, function
downcase_identifier) lowers A to Z and leaves every byte of a multibyte character alone.
With Turkish table names in SQL, quote them or keep them all lower case.

psql's own fold for patterns is cruder. It goes byte by byte through the C library's
`isupper`/`tolower` in the client's locale (src/fe_utils/string_utils.c, function
patternToSQLRegex), which can change a byte inside a UTF-8 letter. Observed with psql 18.7
on StackLab's Windows machine (locale en-US, code page 1252; console code page 437 or 65001;
client encoding UTF8): `\dt Şubeler`, and even `\dt şubeler`, fail with `invalid byte
sequence for encoding "UTF8"`, while `\dt "Şubeler"` and `\dt *ubeler` find the table.
In a pattern, double-quote any name with a non-ASCII letter, lower case included.

## Design notes

psql's split between SQL and meta-commands is the useful lesson here: the database
describes itself in ordinary tables, and every tool, from psql to pgAdmin to your own
health check, is just querying them. When you need schema facts in code (a migration
check, a test asserting an index exists), copy the query `psql -E` shows you, or use
`information_schema` if it must also run on another database. Don't scrape `\d` output:
it is formatted for people and changes between versions.

files.examples/01_list.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.basics.psql): \d and friends are catalog queries; this is one in plain SQL.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email text NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES customers,
  total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE VIEW big_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total >= 1000;
COMMENT ON TABLE orders IS 'One row per checkout';

-- \d with no pattern (= \dtvmsE): the relations visible on the search
-- path, minus the system schemas. \d+ adds size and the COMMENT text.
SELECT c.relname AS "Name",
       CASE c.relkind
         WHEN 'r' THEN 'table'    WHEN 'p' THEN 'partitioned table'
         WHEN 'v' THEN 'view'     WHEN 'm' THEN 'materialized view'
         WHEN 'S' THEN 'sequence' WHEN 'f' THEN 'foreign table'
       END AS "Type",
       pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) AS "Owner",
       obj_description(c.oid, 'pg_class') AS "Description"
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r', 'p', 'v', 'm', 'S', 'f')
  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog', 'information_schema')
  AND n.nspname !~ '^pg_toast'
  AND pg_table_is_visible(c.oid)
ORDER BY "Name";
files.examples/02_describe.sql:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id         int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email      varchar(80) NOT NULL,
  total      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  tags       text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- \d orders, top half: columns with psql's type names and defaults.
SELECT a.attname AS "Column",
       format_type(a.atttypid, a.atttypmod) AS "Type",
       CASE WHEN a.attnotnull THEN 'not null' ELSE '' END AS "Nullable",
       CASE a.attidentity
         WHEN 'a' THEN 'generated always as identity'
         WHEN 'd' THEN 'generated by default as identity'
         ELSE pg_get_expr(d.adbin, d.adrelid)
       END AS "Default"
FROM pg_attribute a
LEFT JOIN pg_attrdef d ON d.adrelid = a.attrelid AND d.adnum = a.attnum
WHERE a.attrelid = 'orders'::regclass
  AND a.attnum > 0 AND NOT a.attisdropped   -- skip system and dropped columns
ORDER BY a.attnum;

-- \d orders, bottom half: constraints. contype 'n' rows are the NOT NULLs,
-- which PG 18 stores here too; the query above already shows them.
SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'orders'::regclass AND contype <> 'n'
ORDER BY conname;

-- The SQL-standard, portable view of the same columns: no modifiers in
-- data_type, and anything Postgres-specific is just 'ARRAY' or 'USER-DEFINED'.
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = current_schema() AND table_name = 'orders'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
files.examples/03_names.sql:
-- psql patterns follow SQL's identifier rules, so look at the names the
-- catalog actually stores before blaming \dt for "missing" tables.
CREATE TABLE Payments (id int);     -- unquoted: folded to lower case
CREATE TABLE "Invoices" (id int);   -- quoted: stored exactly as written
CREATE TABLE Şubeler (id int);      -- unquoted, but Ş is not ASCII

-- 55 characters, 64 bytes: one byte over the identifier limit.
CREATE TABLE iade_talepleri_için_günlük_özet_çizelgesi_ağustos_ölçüm (id int);

SELECT c.relname AS stored_name, length(c.relname) AS chars,
       octet_length(c.relname) AS bytes
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE n.nspname = current_schema() AND c.relkind = 'r'
ORDER BY c.relname;

-- to_regclass returns NULL instead of failing: a quick "does it exist?".
SELECT to_regclass('payments')   IS NOT NULL AS payments,
       to_regclass('PAYMENTS')   IS NOT NULL AS "PAYMENTS",
       to_regclass('invoices')   IS NOT NULL AS invoices,
       to_regclass('"Invoices"') IS NOT NULL AS "quoted Invoices",
       to_regclass('şubeler')    IS NOT NULL AS şubeler;

-- Forget the quotes once and the table "does not exist".
SELECT count(*) FROM Invoices;
